questions.q: Per this lesson, what distinguishes an architecture from a feature list?
options: An architecture is simply a longer feature list
An architecture is only needed for Apex code, not for Flow
An architecture includes the decisions about how pieces are built, why, and how they fit together, not just what the system must do
There is no real difference; the terms are interchangeable
questions.explain: The feature list (Definition of Done) says what the system must do; the architecture is the set of decisions about how and why, and how the pieces connect.

questions.q: Which of these is correctly matched to its architectural layer in this platform?
options: Custom objects for installation and warranty work belong to the Data layer
Role hierarchy and sharing rules belong to the Logic layer
Lightning Web Components belong to the Access layer
Apex triggers belong to the Experience and integration layer
questions.explain: Custom objects are part of the Data layer; role hierarchy/sharing belong to the Access layer, LWCs to the Experience and integration layer, and Apex triggers to the Logic layer.

questions.q: What is this capstone's governing principle for choosing between Flow and Apex?
options: Always prefer Apex because it is more powerful
Use the simplest tool that reliably does the job, reaching for code only when declarative tools genuinely can't handle it
Always prefer Flow and never write Apex under any circumstance
Alternate between Flow and Apex by chapter regardless of the task
questions.explain: The lesson states the rule explicitly: declarative first, with Apex reserved for cases declarative tooling genuinely can't reliably handle, such as the warranty-claim validation at scale.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say the warranty-claim amount validation belongs in an Apex trigger rather than Flow?
options: Because Flow cannot run on the Case object at all
Because Apex triggers are always faster than Flow regardless of the logic
Because Priya personally prefers writing Apex over configuring Flow
Because it needs full control over bulk behavior and a guaranteed, testable order of operations at scale
questions.explain: The lesson gives a specific reason: this is the one piece of logic where Flow genuinely struggles, and the trigger gives full, testable control over bulk behavior and order of operations.

questions.q: Which three non-functional requirements does this lesson say Solstice's platform will be evaluated against?
options: Performance, security, and maintainability
Color scheme, branding, and font choice
Number of custom objects, number of Flows, and number of LWCs
Price, marketing reach, and customer satisfaction surveys
questions.explain: The lesson names performance, security, and maintainability as the three non-functional requirements the finished platform is evaluated against starting in Chapter 4.
